It computes the flag once at Provision from the checked AST and handles dynamic and statically concatenated names well, but it puts reverse_proxy-specific placeholder names in caddyhttp and adds unrequested behavior (recursing into `not` matchers, value-type cases).

Sound AST-based classification with static concatenation support, but the reverse-proxy placeholder list sits in caddyhttp, and the unrequested MatchNot and value-type handling is over-engineered and extends behavior.

The design matches the reference (names plus a dynamic flag extracted at Provision, classification in reverseproxy) and the tests are good, but it accidentally deleted the brokenUpstreamAddr doc comment.
Closely mirrors the reference: it extracts placeholder names and a dynamic flag from the checked AST and classifies them in reverseproxy; the only slip is dropping brokenUpstreamAddr's doc comment.

This is the closest to the reference: it records placeholder names and dynamic usage at Provision, exposes a small generic API, keeps the response-name list in reverseproxy, and adds very thorough tests, including transport-error retry for request expressions.

Records names from the checked AST through a generic MayReferencePlaceholder predicate, which keeps reverse-proxy knowledge in reverseproxy. Tests are thorough: shorthand and direct calls, dynamic names, list/map/comprehension, transport retries still honoring request expressions, and preserved body and status.

Caching response matchers on Handler at Provision means handlers built without Provision never response-retry, which breaks the existing test harness (hidden suite fails); it also moves the CEL regexes into a new internal package and re-parses with a separate parser, which is unnecessary refactoring.

The classification logic is right, but it lives in a new Handler provisioning step, so any handler built without that step silently loses response retries, which is why the hidden tests fail. It also adds an internal package, moves the placeholder regexes, and changes the test helper's signature.

The classification is correct, but it copies the CEL placeholder-expansion regexes and runs regex expansion plus a full CEL parse on every proxied response, which is a hot-path cost and a drift risk; it also rewrote an unrelated existing test's expression and dropped a comment.

Classification is functionally right, but it re-runs regex expansion and CEL parsing on every proxied request in the hot path, duplicates the expansion regexes, and needlessly rewrites an existing test's expression.
